preamble: Depalatalization (hardening) of the palatalized alveolar nasal [nʲ] to plain [n]. Late Common Slavic and Old East Slavic softened consonants before front vowels. Ukrainian later hardened them before /e/, while Russian keeps the soft consonant. Early Czech likewise depalatalized consonants before e and ä, while Polish kept and strengthened the softness.

examples.note: Old East Slavic softened /n/ before /e/ (9th c. /ˈnɛbɔ/ > 11th c. /ˈnʲɛbɔ/); Ukrainian hardened it again, whereas Russian keeps [ˈnʲebə].

examples.from: Old East Slavic нести /nʲɛˈstʲi/ (11th c.) 'to carry'
Proto-Slavic *nebo 'sky', with early West Slavic n’ before e (cf. Polish niebo [ˈɲɛbɔ])
examples.note: Per Wikipedia's History of the Czech language, consonants before e and ä were palatalized in early West Slavic and 'the depalatalization of consonants preceding e and ä took place later' in Czech; Polish keeps the softness.
